newsitem.title: USA: Polls raise hopes for GOP Senate sweep in South.
newsitem.headline: Polls raise hopes for GOP Senate sweep in South.

text.p: Hopes for a Republican sweep of four open U.S. Senate races in the South rose sharply Friday with opinion polls showing Democratic candidates losing ground fast with only four days to go before the election.

Analysts say Republican victories in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia and Louisiana would effectively negate the threat of a Democratic takeover in the Senate, which reverted to the Republicans only two years ago.

Democrats need a net gain of three or four seats to retake the chamber, where Republicans now hold a 53-47 edge. But with Republican candidates gaining ground in all four Southern states, the odds for a shift appeared to be shrinking.

"The Democrats are a long shot to win the Senate anyway. And if they actually have a net loss of three or four (seats) here in the South, they'll have to do phenomenally well in the rest of the country," said Charles Bullock, political scientist at the University of Georgia.
"There aren't a whole lot of instances where you can say the Democrat's going to take out the Republican."

Republicans have always had the chance to sweep the Southern races, where longstanding Democratic incumbents are stepping down at a time when traditionally conservative voters are moving away from their Democratic roots.

Until recently, however, Republicans were expected to lose in Georgia and Louisiana. Experts also believed a close fight in Arkansas would go to the Democrats given a likely presidential win for the state's native son, Bill Clinton.
Only in Alabama, where Republican state Attorney General Jeff Sessions has consistently led Democrat Roger Bedford in opinion polls, was the party able to count on a win.

But all that seemed to change this week with the emergence of two independent polls showing Democratic frontrunners in Georgia and Louisiana falling prey to Republican attack ads casting them as politically liberal and morally corrupt.

Meanwhile, the Washington-based Southern Political Report forecast a narrow Republican victory in Arkansas, where party candidate Tim Hutchinson had tightened his race against Democrat Winston Bryant to a dead heat.
"We've never been in a better position to sweep all four seats," said Gordon Hensley, a spokesman for the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

A Georgia poll, published on Friday by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, showed Democrat Max Cleland trailing Republican Guy Millner by two points, against a 16-point lead a month ago in a survey by the same organisation.

"Georgia is pretty much a Republican state, so Max Cleland is probably fighting for his life. Whatever support he had to begin with was an inch deep and a mile wide," said Bob Stein, political science professor at Rice University in Texas.
In Louisiana, former state Treasurer Mary Landrieu, a moderate Democrat, has seen her lead eroded in a bitter battle against hardline Republican conservative Woody Jenkins.

A poll for WWL-TV in New Orleans showed the pair only five percentage points apart, with Landrieu's support at 45 percent and Jenkins' at 40 percent. "What's happened is that negative campaigning has created more undecided voters. Mary is losing white support," said University of New Orleans political scientist Susan Howell.
Landrieu, whom Jenkins has cast as a soft-on-crime liberal, needs overwhelming black support and about one-third of the white vote, with a heavy turnout among Roman Catholics from southern Louisiana.
